newsitem.title: JAPAN: S.Korean president in Japan, rightists protest.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean president in Japan, rightists protest.

text.p: Hundreds of rightwingers threatened to disrupt the visit by South Korean President Kim Youg-sam when he arrived on Saturday in this hot-springs resort for talks with Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.

Security was tight with nearly 4,000 police on alert for a summit likely to be dominated by nationalistic issues like the "comfort women" affair, female prisoners forced to work as sex slaves for Japan's World War Two military.
Other issues of national pride at state are the co-hosting of the 2002 World Cup and who owns islands both sides claim.
Several hundred rightwingers staged noisy rallies to protest what they described as "unreasonable demands" from South Korea on the issues.

The mood was already tense after Japan's top government spokesman told the Japanese media on the eve of the meeting that there was a "social background" to Tokyo's use of sex slaves during World War Two.
"We must not forgive South Korea for making unreasonable demands," the rightists endlessly shouted through loud speakers on trucks that drove through this small, normally placid town.
"Don't meddle in Japan's internal affairs," was another message.

The rightwingers, ultra nationalist groups who defend Japan's war actions, demanded Kim stop accusing Tokyo of committing atrocities before and during the war, including its 1910-45 colonial rule over the Korean Peninsula.
They urged Hashimoto to stand firm in his talks with Kim.
"Japan must stop its weak-kneed diplomacy," the protestors shouted.
About 200,000 women from Korea, the Philippines, China, Indonesia and the Netherlands were forced to work in front-line brothels in one of the darkest chapters of Japan's World War Two past.

A decades-long row over Japan's failure to fully apologise and pay official compensation to the women flared again earier this month when the Asian Women's Fund, a private group set up in 1995 with heavy Japanese government support, paid five million yen ($4,200) to each of seven ageing Korean women.
South Korea does not want government-to-government compensastion but believes Tokyo should compensate the sex slaves directly.
Japanese rightwing groups regard any softening by Tokyo as a dishonour to ordinary soldiers who fought in the war.
The islands issue is equally emotive.
Japan calls the two small islands Takeshima and South Korea calls them Tokto. They are surrounded by rich fishing grounds.
Tokyo has claimed the islands since it started its 1905 colonial rule of Korea. South Koreans say they have owned the islands for centuries.
On Friday, in potentially explosive remarks reported by Kyodo News Service, Chief Cabinet Secretary Seiroku Kajiyama appeared to indirectly defend some comfort women actions.

"It is odd teaching them (Japanese schoolchildren) of the comfort women issue, without teaching the social background of an authorised prostitution system at that time," the top government spokesman said.
"When they (comfort women) went to the fronts, they got money. Among them, there were some who were drafted," Kajiyama was quoted as saying.
